title: Questions about trees and boosting
objectives: Answer the standard questions on splits, bagging, boosting and feature importance.

screens.title: Score a split
screens.prose: About two minutes a question; say your reasoning aloud first. A tree node holds 10 up days and 10 down days. A split sends 8 up and 2 down to the left. Gini impurity is 1 minus the sum of the squared class shares.

state.caption: The parent node had 10 up days and 10 down days.

screens.question: Fill in the impurities and the gain.

hints.text: Shares in the parent are a half each.
Parent 0.5, each child 0.32, weighted 0.32, gain 0.18.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Square each share, add, and take from 1; the gain is the drop.

explain.text: $1 - 0.64 - 0.04 = 0.32$ for each child. Both hold half the rows, so the weighted impurity is 0.32 and the gain $0.5 - 0.32 = 0.18$.

screens.title: The same split in bits
screens.prose: Score the same split with entropy, $H = -\sum p \log_2 p$. The parent, half and half, has 1 bit.

state.caption: The parent node had 10 up days and 10 down days.

screens.question: What is the information gain?

hints.text: Find the entropy of one child first.
Each child has 0.7219 bits, so the gain is $1 - 0.7219$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the weighted child entropy from 1.

byKey.child: That is the entropy of a child. The gain is the drop from 1 bit.
byKey.gini: That is the Gini gain. Entropy is on another scale.

explain.text: Each child has $H(0.8) = 0.7219$ bits, so the gain is 0.2781. Gini and entropy usually rank splits the same way.

screens.title: Average many trees
screens.prose: Each tree's prediction has variance $\sigma^2 = 4$. Any two trees correlate at $\rho$, because they see similar data. Bagging averages $B$ trees. Slide $\rho$ to see the curve move.
screens.question: With $\rho = 0.3$, what is the variance of the average of 10 trees?

hints.text: Read the curve at $B = 10$ with $\rho = 0.3$.
The shared part $\rho\sigma^2$ never averages away.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the shared part to the part that averages away.

byKey.indep: You divided $\sigma^2$ by 10, as if the trees were independent. Correlated trees average less well.
byKey.floor: That is the floor, reached only as $B$ grows without limit.

explain.text: The average has variance $\rho\sigma^2 + (1 - \rho)\sigma^2/B$. With 10 trees that is 1.48; with 100 trees it is 1.228.

screens.title: The floor
screens.question: What does the variance tend to as $B$ grows without limit?

hints.text: Which term depends on $B$?
The second term, $(1 - \rho)\sigma^2/B$, goes to zero.
What is left is $\rho\sigma^2 = 0.3 \times 4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Let $B$ grow and see which term survives.

byKey.zero: That needs independent trees. Correlation leaves $\rho\sigma^2$ however many trees you add.
byKey.one: That is one tree. Averaging removes the unshared part.

explain.text: Averaging removes only the unshared part. That is why a random forest samples features at each split: it lowers $\rho$ and so the floor.

screens.title: Out of the bag
screens.prose: A bootstrap sample draws 100 rows from 100 with replacement. A row is out of bag if it is never drawn.
screens.question: What share of the 100 rows is out of bag, on average?

hints.text: Each draw misses a given row with chance $1 - 1/100$.
It must miss on all 100 draws.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The row must be missed on every one of the 100 draws.

byKey.inbag: That is the share in the bag, $1 - 0.366$.
byKey.one: That is the chance of missing on one draw only.

explain.text: A row is missed by all 100 draws with chance $0.99^{100} = 0.3660$. So each tree has about a third of the rows to test on: the out-of-bag error.

screens.title: Boost by hand
screens.prose: Four points: (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 6), (4, 7). Start from the mean, 4. Each round fits a one-split stump at $x = 2.5$ to the residuals and adds 0.4 times it.
screens.question: Fill in the predictions after each round.

hints.text: Round 1 residuals are $-3, -2, 2, 3$.
The stump predicts the mean residual on each side: $-2.5$ and $2.5$.
Round 1: $4 \mp 0.4 \times 2.5$ gives 3 and 5. Round 2 residuals average $\mp 1.5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each round adds 0.4 times the mean residual on each side.

explain.text: Round 1 adds $0.4 \times (\mp 2.5)$ to give 3 and 5. The new residuals average $\mp 1.5$, so round 2 gives 2.4 and 5.6. Each round fixes part of what is left.

screens.title: In parallel?
screens.prose: A candidate says: "Boosted trees can be fitted in parallel, like bagged ones."
screens.question: Is that right?

options.text: No: each boosting round fits the residuals of the rounds before, so they run in order.
Yes: each tree is fitted to the same data, so the trees are independent jobs.
options.why: You treated boosting like bagging. A boosting tree is fitted to residuals, which exist only after the previous round.

options.text: Yes, if the learning rate is small, since each round then changes the fit very little.
options.why: The learning rate changes the step, not the order. Round 2 still needs round 1.

options.text: Only with random feature sampling, which makes each tree independent of the others.
options.why: Feature sampling works inside a round. It does not remove the need for the previous residuals.

hints.text: What does round 2 fit?
Round 2 fits the residuals left by round 1.
So round 2 cannot start before round 1 ends.

feedback.correct: Boosting is sequential; bagging is parallel.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what each new boosting tree is trained on.

byKey.yes: That is the trap. Bagged trees share the data and are independent jobs; boosted trees chain on residuals.

explain.text: Bagging trains trees on bootstrap samples of the same data, so they run side by side. Boosting trains each tree on the previous residuals, so it is a chain. Libraries parallelise inside one tree, not across rounds.

screens.title: Who gets the credit
screens.prose: A forest predicts $y = x$ plus noise. The columns are $x$, an exact copy of $x$ and two noise columns. One noise column has 500 integer values.

state.caption: Seeded: $y = x + 0.5\varepsilon$, 1,000 rows, a forest of 200 trees fitted on 700, permutation on the other 300.

screens.question: Select all that apply.

options.text: The two copies share the credit, about half each.
The noise columns earn impurity importance but none on held-out permutation.
The copy carries more information than $x$, since it scores higher on both.
options.why: The copy is exactly $x$, so the information is identical. The gap in the scores is noise in the fit.

options.text: Dropping the copy would lose about 0.47 of the fit.
options.why: The copy is redundant: $x$ alone carries the same information, so the fit barely changes.

hints.text: Compare the two importance columns row by row.
Impurity importance is counted on the training rows.
Copies split the credit; noise wins small training gains that do not hold out.

feedback.correct: Copies share; noise fools impurity importance only.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the copies together and the noise rows across both columns.

explain.text: Impurity importance credits every split, so noise picks up about 0.03 by chance on training rows. Permutation on held-out rows gives it about 0. Copies split the credit, so neither looks as important as $x$ really is.

screens.title: Where the floor comes from
screens.prose: Derive the variance of the average of $B$ trees, each with variance $\sigma^2$ and pairwise correlation $\rho$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: $\text{Var}(\bar{T}) = \frac{1}{B^2}\text{Var}(\sum_b T_b)$, since $\bar{T}$ is a sum over $B$.
The sum has $B$ variances $\sigma^2$ and $B(B - 1)$ covariances $\rho\sigma^2$.
The covariances cancel because the trees are fitted separately.
lines.why: Fitted separately is not independent: they see overlapping data, so the covariances stay.

hints.text: Start from the variance of a sum.
Count the pairs: $B(B - 1)$ ordered pairs.
Divide by $B^2$ and split the $\rho$ term.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Variance of a sum, count the terms, divide, simplify.

byKey.x: You dropped the covariances. Bootstrap samples overlap, so the trees are correlated.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step the derivation needs.

explain.text: The $B$ variances give $\sigma^2/B$ and the $B(B-1)$ covariances give nearly $\rho\sigma^2$. That second piece is the floor no number of trees removes.

screens.title: A signal screen
screens.prose: A forest predicts next-day returns from 40 signals. Ranked by impurity importance, the top one is the stock id, a column with 500 distinct values.

state.caption: Seeded: $y = x + 0.5\varepsilon$, 1,000 rows, a forest of 200 trees fitted on 700, permutation on the other 300.

screens.question: What do you do?

options.text: Recheck by permutation on a later period: many-valued columns win training splits by chance.
Trade on the stock id, since the forest ranks it first of all 40 signals on this data.
options.why: Impurity importance is counted on training rows. A many-valued column can split noise very finely.

options.text: Drop every signal ranked below the stock id, so the model keeps only the strongest.
options.why: The ranking itself is the suspect, so do not prune by it.

options.text: Add more trees until the ranking settles, then trust whichever column comes out on top.
options.why: More trees steady the ranking but keep its bias towards many-valued columns.

hints.text: Look at the 500-value noise row.
Impurity importance is earned on the training data.
Held-out permutation importance does not reward chance splits.

feedback.correct: Test importance out of sample before believing it.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask where impurity importance is measured.

explain.text: Many-valued columns offer many split points, so they win small training gains by chance. Permutation importance on a later period removes that bias.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: The interviewer asks: "Why does a random forest not overfit as you add trees?"
screens.question: Which answer would you give?

options.text: "More trees only average more draws: variance falls to a floor, bias stays. Deep trees can overfit; more trees cannot."
"Because each tree is pruned before it joins the forest, so no tree can fit the noise in its rows."
options.why: Forests often grow deep, unpruned trees. Overfitting comes from the trees, not from their number.

options.text: "Random forests never overfit. Averaging over many bootstrap samples cancels any noise that the trees have fitted."
options.why: Too strong: deep trees on noisy returns can overfit. Only adding trees is safe.

options.text: "Because the out-of-bag error stops it. Each tree is checked on rows it never saw, and bad trees are dropped."
options.why: Out-of-bag error measures the fit; it does not change it.

hints.text: What does the curve do as $B$ grows?
It falls and flattens at $\rho\sigma^2$; it never rises.
Bias comes from tree depth and leaf size, not from $B$.

feedback.correct: More trees lower the variance towards a floor and leave the bias alone.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick the answer that follows the curve.

explain.text: The average of more trees has a variance that falls to $\rho\sigma^2$ and never rises. Bias depends on each tree. So the number of trees is safe; their depth is what to tune.

ideas: Gini is $1 - \sum p^2$; a split scores the drop in weighted impurity.
Bagging $B$ trees gives variance $\rho\sigma^2 + (1 - \rho)\sigma^2/B$, with a floor at $\rho\sigma^2$; boosting chains trees on residuals.
Impurity importance shares credit among copies and rewards noise; check with held-out permutation importance.

formula.name: Variance of a bagged average
formula.note: About $1/e \approx 0.368$ of the rows are out of bag for each tree.

summary.trap: Boosted trees cannot be fitted in parallel like bagged ones: each round needs the residuals of the last.

quiz.prose: A node has 6 up days and 4 down days.
quiz.question: What is its Gini impurity?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Square each share, add, take from 1.

byKey.entropy: That is the entropy in bits. Gini squares the shares.
byKey.share: That is the sum of squared shares. Take it from 1.

explain.text: Shares 0.6 and 0.4 square to 0.36 and 0.16. One minus their sum is 0.48.

quiz.prose: Trees each have variance 1 and pairwise correlation 0.5. You average 20 of them.
quiz.question: What is the variance of the average?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Shared part plus the part that averages away.

byKey.indep: You treated the trees as independent.
byKey.floor: That is the floor; 20 trees leave 0.025 more.

explain.text: $\rho\sigma^2 = 0.5$ stays, and $(1 - \rho)\sigma^2/B = 0.025$ is added. The average has variance 0.525.

quiz.prose: Points (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 6), (4, 7) and a stump at 2.5. Start from the mean 4 with learning rate 1.
quiz.question: After one round, what is the prediction for $x \ge 3$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the whole mean residual on that side.

byKey.lr: That uses learning rate 0.4. With 1 the whole residual mean is added.
byKey.mean: That is the start, before any round.

explain.text: Residuals on the right are 2 and 3, mean 2.5. With learning rate 1 the prediction becomes 6.5 in one step.

quiz.prose: Each tree of a forest is fitted to a bootstrap sample of a large data set.
quiz.question: About what share of rows does a tree never see?

options.text: About 37%
None: every row is drawn
options.why: Sampling with replacement repeats some rows and misses others.

options.text: About 50%
options.why: The chance of missing a row on every draw is $(1 - 1/n)^n \approx 1/e$.

options.text: About 63%
options.why: That is the share it does see.

feedback.generic: Not quite. A row is out of bag if all $n$ draws miss it.

explain.text: Each draw misses a row with chance $1 - 1/n$, so all $n$ miss with chance $(1 - 1/n)^n$. That tends to $1/e$, about 37%.
